Desperate Indians want Batman to take charge. We have reached that stage

All talk of justice is momentary and transient. Arrests are no more than photo opportunities. Would Batman make a difference?

Vir Sanghvi

17 September, 2026 08:00 am IST

Facebook

Follow Us :

Text Size: A- A+

-->

S ometimes people on X, which I still call Twitter, post the strangest things. Amid all the angst and outrage that has dominated my timeline over the past few days, one post stood out: we need Batman here, it said.

Yes, I know it sounds silly because the post did not refer to a new Batman movie (there won’t be one for many months) or a comic book. It referred to Batman himself.

The fictional Batman is an avenger who takes the law into his own hands and goes to places where the justice system does not reach. He knows that the law-and-order machinery is largely corrupt, compromised, incompetent, and ineffectual. So he doles out his own kind of justice, dispensing with the need for due process. At a desperate time, when nothing else works, he is the answer to the prayers of a frustrated citizenry.

Show Full Article

Have we reached that stage in India?

Judging by the people I speak to and those whose social media posts reach me: yes, we have. Things are worse here than they are in Batman’s Gotham City.

Faith in the police is at an all-time low. People believe that involving the cops in any matter may be a mistake because they will just make money from every side and go with what the highest bidder wants. Sadly, this cynicism has now extended to include the judiciary, once regarded as the last hope for justice. Even on routine matters like bail, there is so much cynicism among the public that many judicial decisions nowadays are treated with scepticism.

Indian public is losing trust The discontent and frustration have been building up for years, but the current wave of anger and disgust is due to several recent incidents.

One is the Gurugram hit-and-run case. As can be seen in the now-viral video, a gang of over-muscled rowdy youth in a speeding car deliberately attempts to run over (or, at the very least, hurt and harm) a young woman on a bike. What the video captured is indisputable, but the woman, identified as Shivani Chauhan aka Sia, says she had been subjected to heckling and intimidation by the men in the car even before they banged into her bike. What is also indisputable is that, after hitting her bike, the men sped off.

A public uproar forced the police to take action, but they arrested the driver only after the alcohol (the woman says the men were drunk) had left his bloodstream. Since then, the driver’s lawyer has criticised the woman, and a campaign of vilification aimed at impugning her character has been launched.

All this is bad enough, but what is more disheartening is the consensus among citizens that nothing will come of the case. Once the headlines have faded, some deal will be struck and the youths will be let off, free to run over other women.

There is a recent precedent. A Hindutva ‘activist’ (a word that TV anchors seem to prefer to ‘goonda’) bragged on a podcast about the assault he had committed at the Jantar Mantar protests. He said he could admit it because he was so politically well-connected that nobody could touch him.

The uproar forced the Delhi Police to arrest him. But the ‘activist’ may not have been entirely wrong. Within days, a court granted him bail.

The judge rejected the plea that letting free a man who brags about committing violence could lead to witness intimidation. “In today’s era, intimidation of a victim no longer requires physical proximity,” the judge said. This may or may not be true, but it does make you wonder about the number of people who have been denied bail on the grounds that they could intimidate witnesses. Clearly, the judicial view on the granting of bail varies dramatically from court to court.

Unfortunately for Umar Khalid, who has been denied bail for six years without a trial even beginning, he did not get an enlightened judge like the one this politically well-connected ‘activist’ did.

Also read: BJP’s good times are perhaps ending. But Modi is no Indira Gandhi

The longing for Batman The cynicism about the system mounts each day as more and more revelations emerge. For instance, a pharmacy owner in Bengaluru has been arrested for supplying fake or expired cancer drugs to over 90 pharmacies. The racket has been going on for years, so it is unlikely that a single pharmacy owner was the mastermind. It could not have happened without the connivance of hospital staff and regulators.

When a system allows crooks to profit from cancer patients in a manner that can lead to deaths, it tells you how deep the rot runs.

Is it any wonder that people long for vigilantes like Batman? Nobody has any faith in most politicians. They distrust the police. They are disappointed by the judiciary. And they live in a society where even the drugs given by hospitals to critically ill patients are fake.

What is worse is that we are convinced that justice will never be done. People who are arrested, often only after public outrage and uproar, can buy their way out of criminal charges. Within weeks or a few months, they are back to doing whatever it was that got them arrested.

All talk of justice is momentary and transient. Arrests are no more than photo opportunities. As long as the cops are in the politicians’ good books, their jobs are safe. And their fortunes keep growing.

Would Batman make a difference?

Frankly, I doubt that even if he existed, he could change everything that’s wrong in India. More likely, he would just hang up his cape and cowl and weep silently in the Bat Cave.

Vir Sanghvi is a print and television journalist, and talk show host. He tweets @virsanghvi. Views are personal.

(Edited by Prashant Dixit)

By Kanishka Singh Sept 16 (Reuters) – Pop star Ed Sheeran said the decision to drop pro-Palestinian rapper Macklemore from his U.S. concert tour was made by organisers, not him, after he failed to defuse the latest show-business furore over the Gaza conflict.

Macklemore, a longtime critic of Israel’s assault on Gaza, was axed from the U.S. leg of Sheeran’s Loop Tour after his “Free Palestine” remarks during a concert earlier this month in New Jersey triggered a backlash.

The devastation in Gaza, following militant group Hamas’ October 7, 2023 attack on Israel, has spawned multiple controversies in the entertainment and publishing worlds, with pro-Palestinian, Jewish and Israeli personalities all saying they have lost work as a result of their stances.

Show Full Article

Venue owners said they would not allow a concert with Macklemore in the lineup.

“I spoke with the venues at length all week to try and build a bridge … I was also involved in direct talks with promoters along with activists on both sides to try and find a mutual resolution for all, but the venue’s and promoter’s decision was final,” Sheeran said on Tuesday via X.

“Macklemore coming off tour was the promoter’s decision, it was not mine.”

In solidarity with Macklemore, Sheeran’s opening acts – including musician Finneas, Danish band Lukas Graham and singer-songwriter Aaron Rowe – and his band Beoga are leaving the tour.

“Artists must not be silenced when they speak up for the oppressed,” Finneas said, while Rowe and Beoga cited their nation Ireland’s history under colonization to explain their decision.

Pro-Israeli groups and American singer Pink, who is Jewish, have said Macklemore’s comments risk compromising the safety of Jewish and pro-Israeli people at events. Pink last week specifically criticized those using the word “Zionist” as a slur. Beoga, in its statement following its exit from the tour this week, said Macklemore was being silenced by “zionist lobbies.”

She and others also noted a 2014 appearance where Macklemore donned a costume that included a black wig, beard and a fake hooked nose, which critics said tapped into antisemitic stereotypes.

Macklemore later apologised for that incident.

SHEERAN: ‘I AM NOT COMPLICIT’

Sheeran said he was appalled by the conflict between Israel and Palestinians but wanted his concerts to be a place of unity, joy, escapism and love – free of politics.

“I am not complicit. I have my personal views on this devastating conflict. Just because I choose not to speak publicly, it doesn’t mean I don’t have them, and it doesn’t mean I don’t care. Nor does it mean I don’t support causes in my own, personal way,” he said.

“Those who come to my shows do not expect a political forum. I respect Macklemore’s strength of purpose to stand up and shout for what he believes. However, there is room for multiple approaches to the same end: peace.”

Macklemore, a Grammy-winning artist, had been due to perform at eight of 10 shows Sheeran has left on his stadium tour, which is to resume on September 19 in Philadelphia.

“A big part of the reason why I wanted to do this tour in the first place is so I could stand up in stadiums like this and say two words that are very near and dear to my heart: ‘Free Palestine,'” Macklemore said earlier this month.

“I want those words to be loud and clear, so that people all the way in Gaza to the occupied West Bank know that we have not forgotten about them.”

Sheeran said those he had spoken to in search of a solution included billionaire Robert Kraft, owner of Gillette Stadium outside Boston, where Sheeran is scheduled to perform in a pair of shows later this month. Kraft in a statement said Macklemore would not perform at those shows.

Macklemore said Sheeran told him that Kraft rallied other stadium owners to do the same, a claim Kraft has not publicly addressed.

(Reporting by Kanishka Singh in Washington; additional reporting by Louise Breusch Rasmussen and Chandini Shah; editing by Andrew Cawthorne Stephen Coates)
